podcasts.name: The MAD Podcast with Matt Turck
podcasts.title: Who Feeds the GPUs? Inside AI's Hidden $30B Layer | Renen Hallak, VAST Data
podcasts.transcript: Sometimes it scares me. We had a customer, one of these AI clouds. They said, "We're probably going to need about 500 pabytes over the next three years." Last week, they came back to us and said, "We're going to need an extra 2 exabytes on top of that 500 pabytes." I think in the next 10 years, we'll see more difference than we did in the last thousand years. Hi, I'm Met. Welcome to the Matt podcast. We talk a lot about AI models on this show and we talk a lot about compute, but today is about the layer in between, the crucial software infrastructure layer that feeds massive amounts of data to all those GPUs. My guest today is Renan Hock, founder and CEO of Vast Data, a company that is surprisingly under the radar considering it's been most recently valued at $30 billion and powers top AI players like XAI and some of the biggest AI neocads in the world. Please enjoy my conversation with Randon Hock. Renan welcome. >> Thank you. >> All right. So to anchor this whole conversation uh I wanted to start with um that mental model from Jensen at Nvidia that I I find so helpful where uh when he describes AI uh he uses the analogy of a five layer cake uh where you have power at the very bottom and then hardware then software infrastructure then models then applications. So where do you sit in that layer cake? >> Right in the middle. That software infrastructure layer is the one that we do uh in collaboration of course with the hardware vendors underneath us and with the model builders on top of us. >> Yeah. So at a at a high level what does that mean software infrastructure in the context of AI building? >> Yeah. So everything you would imagine from the old stack we need for this new stack. We need to manage the compute. We need to manage the storage. we need to manage the networking and then as you go up the stack we need to make sense of all of it. Uh make sense of the data through a database, make sense of the compute through training and inference functions. Um and as you go even higher up the stack and we shift from training predominantly to inference and agents and uh reinforce learning, we need more and more tools to enable this new world. Make it simple, make it safe, make it um fast and scalable and resilient. All of that sits in that middle layer. Uh sometimes I like to call it software infrastructure and other times I like to call it the operating system for this new era. There is a related concept to that five layer cake that think may have originated from Nvidia again but like keeps coming back in conversation which is this idea of AI factory. >> Mh. >> What does that mean? So if you start with a bunch of GPUs, what do you need to add to create a an AI factory? >> I think even below the GPUs, the data centers are looking very different today than they did 5 years ago. The old stack you had 10 kow racks. Today you need 500 kilowatt racks. And so you need more power. You need more power density. Um you need GPUs of course versus CPUs. you need extremely fast networks and very large SSDs rather than 10 gig Ethernet and old hard drives. And so every layer of this cake uh needs to be redone. And from our perspective, you need much more data and much faster access to that data because we're no longer analyzing numbers and columns of a database the way you did with big data in the old stack. We're doing pictures and video and sound and natural language and that takes a lot more space and that's before new generative AI data uh that gets generated and of course all of this uh compute all of these GPUs need very fast access to this information whether they're training on it or whether they're running uh low latency inference functions and so the entirety of the stack is new and I think the culmination of this stack is what we call the AI factory. >> And is the concept of AI factory uh mostly for the the big labs or like this whole like data center plus model kind of kind of thing or um is it also for enterprises? >> I think it'll be for everyone eventually. Uh the big labs are starting. They're ahead of the pack and they're leading the way for everybody else. But anybody who stays with the old stack with old business information systems will get left behind. And so people need to start leveraging these new AI abilities. Some uh start by leveraging them out of the clouds, out of the hyperscalers, the neoclouds. Um others build uh within their environments. Um but in all of these cases enterprises will need AI factories in the medium term and then after that I think as we shift from people uh based organizations to augmenting them with agents these AI factories become a lot more uh than what we're used to thinking from just our compute infrastructure to play it back right now if you go to a large enterprise a non techch enterprise so like fizer or gold tax or Walmart. Um I think the the dominant view is that um leveraging AI basically means uh you know you start partnering with enthropic or open AI and you know you have FDS coming into your walls and then you know you you build some stuff initially that was chatbots now it's agents is is a concept of an AI factory that you build your own AI so you you have uh your own you know data infrastructure but you also rent you GPUs or buy GPUs and then you you do model work. Is that is that the concept? I think once you get to a certain level of scale definitely it's more cost effective to buy than to rent and so from that perspective yes you should build your own uh AI factories but beyond that over time I think all of these organizations IP will be distilled in models uh it will be weights and they don't necessarily need to build the base model I like to give analogies of of the human brain we were all born with a base model but then over time as we uh travel the world, we learn new things. Uh we infer during the day, we fine-tune at night, and tomorrow we'll be a little bit smarter than we were today. And my model of the universe is slightly different than your model of the universe because we had different experiences. And so I think in the same way, all of these agents will fine-tune models through reinforced learning over time. and every organization's IP will be able to be um distilled into the models that they own and the weights that they've accumulated. >> What does that mean in terms of what those enterprises need to be able to do? You know, like doing model work and like weights and GPUs that that's a whole kind of expertise that ultimately few people in the world already own uh or already know have. uh and then a lot of those companies just don't have that. So how do they go from here to there? >> I think again I like analogies. The analogy I would give here is you go back to the 1970s you needed a PhD in computer science to operate a computer. Today everybody can do it. And the reason everybody can do it is not because we learned. It's because operating a computer became much simpler. uh the operating system made it intuitive, made it easy for everybody to use. Uh it also made it safe for everybody to use. These enterprises are under a lot of regulation that they need to comply with. And so uh it is our job as the ones building that software infrastructure layer to make these new technologies accessible to the enterprises such that they don't need to think about it too much and that they can start adopting them at pace um rather than get left behind and have new companies with AI experts uh take their place. maybe to push back a little bit or maybe to just dig in to make sure I understand that's the whole premise of the cloud is to make things incredibly simple and and and and use those functionality as a service. The concept of an AI factory revolves around owning a lot of this. So it sounds like very kind of like onrem private cloud uh which historically has been a lot more complicated. So is effectively what you're saying that uh is that like there's an opportunity to like abstract away all of this in a way that that feels cloudish in experience. >> I think so. I think uh the physical location of this AI factory can be on prem uh can be in a colo can be in an AI cloud uh where you rent it from somebody rather than manage it yourself. Eventually my guess is that the hyperscalers will also enable these AI factories to be built uh within their premises. Um, but so long as it's within your control and so long as you're the one that owns it in terms of really I think owns the information, owns the models, owns the weights, owns the agents. I think that's the distinction that I'm trying to make here. Doesn't necessarily need to be physical equipment within a building that belongs to you. >> Okay. Great. Great. Do you want to spend more time on what you alluded to a minute ago about agents and agents doing their own fine-tuning? I mean, right right now the way I think most people think about agents is that uh you know you do reinforcement learning to enable the agents, but I think you're saying agents do it. I again like to think of agents as artificial people and over time I think we're all going to have agents that work for us. uh whether we're people or organizations uh for different tasks and we'll have teams of agents that can help us develop software or uh personalized medicine or whatever it is that we want done we will have them do on our behalf and I think over time we will get attached to our agents and we will expect them to know things that happened yesterday or that happened a year ago and that will allow us familiarity with our agents but that requires them to fine-tune models based on experiences that they had with us. Um, and of course that also makes them smarter and able to do more for us and within teams they can learn from each other and I think that generates the next level of artificial intelligence versus where we are today where everybody is based on some base model from one big lab or another and every few weeks we get an upgrade to that model based on what they did uh in their environment. um in this new way each one of us, each organization owns the IP generated through these uh fine-tuning mechanisms rather than letting the big model builders basically own everything over time. >> Okay. So just to play it back so that the knowledge loop happens within the enterprise and that becomes the new IP and so we saying you cannot do that with openthropic or whoever you don't want to because you don't want to expose your proprietary information your processes your secret sauce uh out to somebody else such that they can take it and run with it >> which is uh super interesting right because people used to say that about data but now we saying this about um >> intelligence >> intelligence processes and memory and therefore intelligence okay does that mean that opensource uh becomes the the play here because if you want to uh fine-tune or do RL against a model um you know having access to an open source model enables you to to do that so is that your vision of the world >> not necessarily I think we need to build a way for people to monetize uh these abilities that they worked so hard and paid so much uh to get to and and so we need a way where on the one hand an enterprise does not expose their data on the other hand a model builder does not expose their weights and again the software infrastructure layer is the right place to enforce that type of trust. Um, and over time as the enterprise starts to generate their own models or fine-tune on top of base models, they should also be able to monetize the skill sets that they develop. And so if I run a carpentry shop and my uh carpenter robots are the best in the business, I should be able to lease to you that brain module such that you can build a chair or whatever it is that you're trying to do. um but I'm only giving it to you for a week and at the end of that week you don't have access to it anymore or maybe I'm selling it to you uh but I still don't want you to see those weights and so there should be ways for us to build a intelligence marketplace. >> Okay. And um I guess that goes to uh your big announcement of of this week. uh do you want to mention the the principle of it and then we we'll go into the the details in a minute but at a at a high level um how does what you guys just announced address this specific problem. >> Sure. So basically what we're trying to do is fill out that software infrastructure layer and what we've realized was that the five layer cake that we discussed is almost complete. The models don't really live on top of the software infrastructure. models over time have become a resource just like a GPU is a resource or an SSD is a resource and resources need to be managed and so this announcement is all about model management. How do we as the operating system now get an understanding of this model is really good at coding and that model is really good at generating images and this one is expensive and that one is inexpensive and that way we can uh understand which tasks belong under which models and that's today when we have four or five of them as we start to reinforce uh running reinforce learning and fine-tune as we start to have hundreds and thousands of agents uh and over time generating new derivatives of those models that's going to be a much bigger task. uh one specific aspect of model management which uh we're announcing and we have a lot of the model builders as partners join the announcement is around confidential computing and enabling that ability of enterprises to run inference on prem without exposing uh the model builder's weights and so both sides can rest assured that my data is not exposed and your weights are not exposed to me and so with help from Nvidia and uh encrypted memory underneath, we're able to make sure that no one sees what they're not allowed to see and to hopefully increase the total addressable market of these model builders into regulated industries into uh large enterprises that are uh careful with their sensitive information. Let's put a pin in this and we'll revisit in a few minutes and go into how that actually works. But uh taking a a step back um uh I would love to um talk about your journey a little bit and and and and then how it led to you to build vast which is this uh incredible company which is valued at $30 billion that you know interestingly perhaps because you're right in the middle of the of the cake not everybody has has heard about yet. Um, so, uh, I think you were telling me, uh, growing up in Israel that you had a particular affinity for, for math. So, my words, not yours, but like you were a bit of a of a whiz kid, uh, in in in in math. >> Affinity for math for sure. Whiz kid, definitely not. Uh, it's funny when I came up here, the math museum is downstairs, and we had some big news this week about math. Um when I was in school 20 years ago, I spent uh 6 months of my life trying to figure out if P equals NP. Uh which I hope your audience knows, but for those who don't, it's the question of is it easier to uh verify a problem than it is to solve the problem, which intuitively it is. It's much easier for us to review a document and say, "Yeah, that's uh that works." than to write that document or to look at a picture and say that's beautiful than to paint that picture. Um but mathematically it's unknown if if that is the case or not. And interestingly this is one of seven millennium problems that the Clay Institute back in the year 2000 put a million dollar bounty on. And I remember spending those six months trying to solve it because I thought if I prove that P does equal NP, then I also solve the other six and I'll get $7 million. And if I prove that it's not equal, then at least I get one. And after 6 months, what I realized was that I'm not nearly smart enough to do it. >> Do you want to provide the the full context about what happened this week just uh for for anybody that didn't follow? Uh, another one of those problems, Navy Stokes, was solved by OpenAI, or at least they claim that they've solved it. And the rumors are hopefully by the time that this is aired, uh, some of those rumors will come true that there's at least two more of the seven problems that OpenAI and Anthropic are trying to solve and are close to solving using AI. And these are problems that have been open for nearly a hundred years. And for the last 26 years, uh there was a million-dollar uh prize associated with them and still people were not able to solve. And so for the first time, I think we're at a point today where AI has proven that it can do things that we don't know how to do. Um, but going back 20 years, it was clear to me that if we could get computers uh to help with these hard problems, that's the way to solve it. Because people are slow and the evolution of our knowledge is slow. And if we are to see any of these things get solved uh within our lifetime, we need computers to speed us up. Um, we didn't know how to do it back in 2006. And so I went along my way and joined a few technology companies. Uh the last one I was with was a company called EMC uh which build large storage systems. >> And if I recall correctly, so you joined a startup as employee number one >> stream.io. Yes. >> And that company was acquired by EMC. That's right. And then you help run that the R&D organization within EMC for that product. >> And that acquisition happened in 2012. And by 2015 um it became clear that there is a shot at computers uh helping us think and helping us solve problems. Uh because neural nets which again when I was in school 10 years earlier or 15 years earlier were a curiosity. They didn't really weren't able to do anything. Uh now they were for the first time starting to show that they can do something. Um and so immediately I tried to figure out how this happened and it was very clear that it wasn't necessarily new algorithms. It was giving those neural nets much faster access to a lot more data that enabled them to perform these very simple tasks. >> So that was the intuition behind the founding of VAST. >> Correct. I >> 2015 >> 2015 beginning of 2016 we started. >> Yeah. So what was the uh the idea then because there were not a lot of customers using massive amounts of data for AI at the time? >> There was no generative AI at the time. Uh Google acquired Deep Mind a year previous to that. Um but it was clear that none of the systems, none of the infrastructure that we had available to us would be scalable enough, would be performant enough to enable this next revolution. The architectures were built on an assumption that things needed to be fast or big. Uh and here you needed something that was both fast and very very large. And so we needed to build a new underlying uh layer to enable the success of this next revolution if if it were to come to fruition. Uh in the early days of course our customers were not doing generative AI, they were doing large scale analytics. They were doing um autonomous driving projects. They were doing medical imaging uh analysis, genomics analysis. Uh >> traditional scientific computing. Oh, hedge funds obviously. Right. >> Yeah. And actually as as a way of getting into what VAST actually does um do do you want to explain in in super simple terms um what you just said? So uh so you started from storage uh and then storage as you just said was it's either the alternative at the time was either slow and inexpensive or fast but expensive and the whole uh scientific kind of breakthrough is to break this right and um uh was it what you called days >> disagregated shared everything >> all right so explain that in in super simple terms >> so the old way to build scalable systems is based on a concept called sharding. Uh what's known as shared nothing systems where you have a lot of nodes. Each node is responsible for a piece of the pie. They collaborate with each other in order to serve up application requests. And as you add more nodes, you get more performance. You get more capacity. It works well up to a certain limit. And so once you have too many nodes, the communication between them starts to show diminishing returns. And so if you're analyzing text, uh it may work. If you're analyzing numbers, it works well. If you're analyzing columns of a database, that's fine. Once you grow beyond that, and today the amounts of data are four, five orders of magnitude beyond where they were back then, soon they will be seven, eight orders of magnitude bigger. Um it doesn't work. It breaks down because uh the communication grows quadratically within the cluster. And then um from a resilience perspective also when one part fails everybody needs to recover that takes time. You can't really have more than a 100 nodes in one of those systems. Uh to build AI we need systems with many millions of nodes. Uh we have one system uh at one of our customer sites that is today multiple exabytes within a single cluster uh delivering tens of terabytes per second. This is tens of thousands of nodes even today before the agentic revolution. And so to do that, we needed to build an architecture that ended up being the opposite of the way shared nothing systems work. Instead of having the SSDs, the media directly attached to the CPU, it's on the other side of the network. And that through a very fast network and through new protocols like NVMe over fabrics and through new media types that allow us to save not just data on the other side of the network but also met metadata. Uh we were able to have all of the nodes uh see all of the information as if it was directly attached. And that's what led us to being able to do what we call shared everything. All of the nodes now don't need to communicate with each other because they share access to all of the information. That's the basic idea behind our architecture. And it proved really really good for a new type of storage system for AI and then for a new type of database for AI and then for a new way to orchestrate compute for AI.
